posts.name: The Kobeissi Letter
posts.text:
China’s industrial profit growth is losing momentum:

China’s industrial profits rose +4.2% YoY in August, the weakest YoY growth since November 2025.

This also marks the 4th consecutive monthly slowdown in growth.

Pressure is particularly visible in consumer-facing industries, where profits are falling in autos, clothing, and furniture.

Domestic demand continues to weaken, with consumption growth slowing to near zero while manufacturers, property developers, and infrastructure builders are cutting spending.

For the first 8 months of 2026, industrial profits were still up +15.7% YoY, but the gains are becoming increasingly concentrated, with the electronics industry contributing ~66% of total growth.

At the same time, raw-material industries contributed +6.2 percentage points to the overall increase, supported by higher commodity prices.

Weak domestic demand is weighing on China’s economy.

posts.name: Carl Quintanilla
Lance Roberts
posts.text:
Fair context, Luke, and I agree the starting point is worse. Full-employment deficits near 6% of GDP, NIIP near -90%, and a larger offshore dollar short all raise the term premium and the risk of fiscal-credibility shocks. No argument there.

But I'd push back on "every crisis since." The 10-yr bottomed in Aug 2020, after the recession ended in April, and rose on recovery and 9% inflation. In the SVB crisis yields fell sharply. In the Aug 2024 yen carry unwind they fell again. April 2025 is the real counterexample, and I'd grant that one. But it was a basis-trade unwind over days, not a recession.

On NIIP, a large share of the deterioration is valuation. Foreigners own far more US equities, and US stocks have outperformed. Equity liabilities aren't a funding need the way debt is.

And a bigger offshore dollar short means a sharper dollar squeeze in a crisis, which means foreigners buying dollars. That's what the swap lines are built for.

So I'd frame it this way. These factors make yields more vulnerable during expansions and inflation scares. They haven't yet overridden the collapse in private demand that drives yields down in an actual recession.
